questions.stem: Which statement defines an enzyme’s role as a catalyst?

options.text: It increases reaction rate without being used up
options.why: An enzyme can take part in repeated catalytic cycles because it’s regenerated after product release.

options.text: It supplies the chemical energy required by reactants
options.why: Enzymes don’t supply energy. They lower the activation-energy barrier for a reaction.

options.text: It changes the reaction’s products into lower-energy substances
options.why: A catalyst doesn’t change which products form or their energy. It changes the pathway and rate.

options.text: It shifts the equilibrium permanently toward product formation
options.why: Enzymes speed forward and reverse reactions without changing the equilibrium position.

options.text: Formation of glycogen from glucose monomers
options.why: This builds a polysaccharide from smaller molecules, so it’s anabolic.

options.text: Synthesis of a polypeptide from amino acids
options.why: This constructs a macromolecule and requires an energy input, so it’s anabolic.

options.text: Oxidation of glucose during cell respiration
options.why: Respiration breaks down and oxidizes an organic substrate, releasing energy for cellular use.

options.text: Production of carbohydrates during photosynthesis
options.why: Photosynthesis builds carbon compounds using an energy input, so it’s anabolic.

options.text: The enzyme and substrate change conformation as they interact
options.why: Binding causes conformational changes that position catalytic groups and make reaction more likely.

options.text: The rigid active site admits every substrate of the correct size
options.why: Active sites aren’t rigid, and binding depends on chemical properties as well as size.

options.text: The substrate changes permanently before reaching the active site
options.why: The interaction begins when the substrate binds. Product formation follows inside the enzyme–substrate complex.

options.text: The enzyme unfolds completely and wraps around its substrate
options.why: Induced fit is a limited conformational change. Complete unfolding would disrupt the active site.

questions.stem: Why is an enzyme-catalyzed reaction slow at a low temperature?

options.text: Substrates permanently occupy all available active sites
options.why: That describes saturation at high substrate concentration. It isn’t an effect of low temperature.

options.text: The enzyme’s peptide bonds are hydrolyzed by cold
options.why: Low temperature doesn’t normally hydrolyze the enzyme’s primary structure.

options.text: Molecules move more slowly, producing fewer successful collisions
options.why: Lower kinetic energy reduces collision frequency and the proportion of collisions with enough energy.

options.text: The reaction develops a larger overall energy change
options.why: Temperature doesn’t explain the low rate by changing the energy difference between reactants and products.

questions.stem: A reaction rate stops increasing at a very high substrate concentration. What limits the rate?

options.text: The availability of unoccupied enzyme active sites
options.why: The enzymes are saturated, so enzyme concentration limits how many catalytic cycles can occur per second.

options.text: The substrate’s inability to move through the solution
options.why: Substrate molecules still move and collide. Most active sites are already occupied as often as possible.

options.text: The denaturation of enzymes by substrate collisions
options.why: Frequent substrate collisions don’t explain this plateau. Active-site saturation does.

options.text: The disappearance of activation energy from the reaction
options.why: The reaction still has an activation-energy barrier. The enzyme lowers it but doesn’t remove it.

questions.stem: A student records oxygen volume every 10 seconds during a catalase reaction. How should the initial reaction rate be found?

options.text: Divide the final oxygen volume by the final temperature
options.why: Temperature isn’t the time interval. This calculation can’t produce a reaction rate.

options.text: Find the gradient of the oxygen-volume graph near time zero
options.why: The initial gradient gives change in product volume per unit time before conditions change substantially.

options.text: Average all oxygen volumes without using elapsed time
options.why: A mean volume isn’t a rate because it contains no change per unit time.

options.text: Use the steepest gradient after the reaction has finished
options.why: After the reaction finishes, the gradient approaches zero. The initial section supplies the initial rate.

questions.stem: Which statement about enzyme activation energy is accurate?

options.text: The enzyme lowers the energy of both reactants and products
options.why: Their energy levels remain unchanged. The enzyme lowers the barrier between them.

options.text: The enzyme provides an alternative pathway with a lower barrier
options.why: More reacting molecules can overcome the lower activation-energy barrier at the same temperature.

options.text: The enzyme raises molecular kinetic energy without heating
options.why: Enzymes don’t increase kinetic energy. Their effect comes from an alternative reaction pathway.

options.text: The enzyme removes the need to weaken substrate bonds
options.why: Substrate bonds still need to be strained, weakened or broken during reaction.

questions.stem: Which pair contains one linear and one cyclical metabolic pathway, in that order?

options.text: Krebs cycle and glycolysis
options.why: The order is reversed. The Krebs cycle is cyclical, while glycolysis is linear.

options.text: Calvin cycle and Krebs cycle
options.why: Both regenerate an acceptor molecule and are cyclical pathways.

options.text: Glycolysis and Krebs cycle
options.why: Glycolysis converts an initial substrate through a linear sequence, while the Krebs cycle regenerates an acceptor.

options.text: Glycolysis and protein digestion
options.why: Glycolysis is linear, but protein digestion isn’t the required example of a cyclical pathway.

questions.stem: Why can increasing substrate concentration overcome competitive inhibition?

options.text: Substrate binding permanently changes the inhibitor’s structure
options.why: The inhibitor doesn’t need to be chemically changed. Substrate and inhibitor compete through reversible binding.

options.text: More substrate increases its chance of occupying the active site
options.why: At high substrate concentration, substrate is more likely than inhibitor to bind during each available opportunity.

options.text: Extra substrate creates additional allosteric sites on the enzyme
options.why: Substrate concentration doesn’t create binding sites. Competitive inhibition occurs at existing active sites.

options.text: More substrate converts competitive inhibition into non-competitive inhibition
options.why: The inhibitor’s binding site and mechanism don’t change when substrate concentration rises.

questions.stem: Why can’t extra substrate restore the original maximum rate during non-competitive inhibition?

options.text: The inhibitor has permanently hydrolyzed every substrate molecule
options.why: A non-competitive inhibitor acts on the enzyme, not by destroying all substrate.

options.text: The inhibitor occupies the active site more strongly than substrate
options.why: That describes competition at the active site. A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere.

options.text: Allosteric binding leaves fewer enzymes with functional active sites
options.why: The inhibitor changes active-site conformation, so extra substrate can’t make those inhibited enzymes catalyze normally.

options.text: The added substrate lowers the solution temperature below optimum
options.why: Adding substrate doesn’t inherently lower temperature. The rate stays reduced because of enzyme conformation.

questions.stem: How does accumulated isoleucine regulate its own synthesis?

options.text: It hydrolyzes threonine before the pathway can begin
options.why: Isoleucine regulates an enzyme. It doesn’t remove threonine by hydrolysis.

options.text: It irreversibly binds to every enzyme in the pathway
options.why: Feedback inhibition is reversible and targets an early regulatory enzyme rather than every enzyme.

options.text: It competes with threonine for the first active site
options.why: The required mechanism is allosteric feedback inhibition, not active-site competition with threonine.

options.text: It binds allosterically to threonine deaminase and slows the first step
options.why: The end product inhibits the first enzyme, reducing pathway activity until isoleucine concentration falls.

questions.stem: What is the direct effect of penicillin binding to bacterial transpeptidase?

options.text: Irreversible enzyme inactivation and reduced peptidoglycan cross-linking
options.why: Penicillin forms a covalent attachment at the active site, so transpeptidase can’t catalyze normal wall cross-linking.

options.text: Reversible competition followed by increased wall synthesis
options.why: Penicillin’s mechanism-based inhibition is irreversible, and wall cross-linking decreases.

options.text: Immediate hydrolysis of every existing peptidoglycan strand
options.why: Penicillin blocks new cross-linking. It doesn’t directly digest every existing strand.

options.text: Allosteric activation of enzymes that produce bacterial membranes
options.why: Penicillin inhibits a cell-wall transpeptidase at its active site. It doesn’t activate membrane synthesis.
